title: Changing who bears environmental cleanup risk changes firms' pollution and loan terms
source_unit: CES-26-05 using EPA environmental data matched to Census establishment and firm microdata and Dealscan loan records
geography: United States; establishments inside and outside the Eleventh Circuit before and after the 1996 federal Lender Liability Act

observations.period: 1992-1999 establishment and loan outcomes around the 1996 Lender Liability Act; paper published January 2026

pollution.value: After lender environmental liability was narrowed, treated establishments increased on-site CERCLA pollution by about 15% on the intensive margin and 2% on the extensive margin

abatement.value: Treated establishments reduced process-related abatement activity by about 14.7%

unexpected_release.value: Treated establishments were about 25% more likely to experience an unexpected environmental release relative to baseline

loan_contract.value: Following the legal change, secured-debt maturity increased about 17% for affected firms; higher lender liability is associated with less favorable pricing and shorter maturity that can support monitoring

economic_distortion.value: The paper reports small production and employment distortions from lender environmental responsibility

air_pollution_counterexample.value: Effects are close to zero and statistically insignificant for air releases, which are outside the CERCLA contamination mechanism used in the design

observations.method: The paper uses a difference-in-differences design comparing establishments inside the Eleventh Circuit, where a 1990 capacity-to-control standard had expanded lender liability, with establishments elsewhere before and after the 1996 federal Lender Liability Act. EPA, Census, and Dealscan records are linked at establishment-chemical-year and loan-facility-year levels with fixed effects and firm controls.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The legal shock identifies a specific secured-lending and CERCLA setting in 1990s establishments; it does not measure all pollution, all lenders, household exposure, local health, cleanup completion, or current sustainable-finance practice. Establishment records do not identify the same residents or workers over time.
observations.subgroup: Establishments by Eleventh Circuit status, secured-debt use, asset location, financial distress, chemical, industry, and pollution type; loan outcomes distinguish secured facilities and high-pollution firms.
observations.counterinterpretation: The estimates are consistent with lender incentives and monitoring, but other circuit-specific or post-1996 changes could matter; the paper uses pre-trends, unaffected air pollution, secured-debt intensity, and adjacent-circuit checks to strengthen the design. More favorable credit terms or longer maturity can support production while weakening environmental discipline; reported production and employment distortions do not establish worker or community wellbeing.

boundary: This record adds a bounded lender-liability-to-firm-environmental-practice pathway. It does not establish current pollution exposure, health harm, cleanup outcomes, household burden, or a universal role for finance in environmental governance.
